The society also opposed a planned rollback of anesthesia-specific quality measures, including one tracking postoperative nausea and vomiting prevention. Final CY 2027 regulations are expected around November 1, with any changes effective January 1, 2027. ASA · ASA Challenges Flawed Payment Proposals From CMS for 2027 GE HealthCare Issues an Urgent Correction for Aisys/Datex-Ohmeda Machines After Anesthetic Delivery Interruptions The FDA has classified a GE HealthCare correction for Aisys and Datex-Ohmeda anesthesia delivery systems as a Class 2 recall (initiated July 30, posted to the FDA database September 16). Affected units contain electronic gas-mixer assemblies that can automatically transition the machine into Alternate O2 Control: the system keeps delivering 100% oxygen and audible/visual alarms sound, but volatile anesthetic agent delivery stops until a clinician intervenes. GE attributes the defect to a nonconforming component and has notified customers directly; the agency warns that an unrecognized transition could leave a patient under-anesthetized mid-case. Facilities running affected Aisys/Datex-Ohmeda units should confirm they've received and actioned GE's correction letter. Postoperative delirium occurred in 7.3% of the hypotension-avoidance group versus 7.0% of the hypertension-avoidance group (RR 1.04; 95% CI, 0.79–1.38) — no meaningful difference. At one year, clinically significant cognitive decline (a drop of more than two points on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment) was seen in 37.2% versus 33.1% (RR 1.13; 95% CI, 0.92–1.38), also not statistically significant. For SRNAs, the practical takeaway is that neither strategy has been shown to meaningfully protect cognition in this population — so the choice of intraoperative blood-pressure target for a patient on chronic antihypertensives should still rest on hemodynamic and surgical considerations rather than an assumed neuroprotective edge. Context-sensitive half-time is the time needed for plasma drug concentration to fall by 50% after stopping an infusion, as a function of how long ("the context") the infusion has run — and it behaves very differently from a drug's elimination half-life. Fentanyl's context-sensitive half-time climbs steeply with infusion duration because the drug keeps redistributing into a large, slowly-equilibrating peripheral compartment (fat and muscle) that becomes an ever-larger reservoir the longer the infusion continues; after a few hours, fentanyl's effective offset can rival that of a drug with a much longer terminal half-life. Remifentanil is the exception that makes the concept click: its context-sensitive half-time stays flat at roughly 3–5 minutes regardless of infusion duration, because it's metabolized by nonspecific plasma and tissue esterases rather than redistribution or hepatic clearance — the same enzymatic pathway keeps clearing it at a constant rate no matter how much drug has accumulated in peripheral tissue. That's the pharmacologic basis for using remifentanil infusions in cases where rapid, predictable emergence matters, and for the clinical reality that a remifentanil infusion must be backed up with longer-acting analgesia before it's stopped, or the patient will be in significant pain within minutes. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History October 6, 1905 On October 6, 1905, Dr. A. F. Erdmann invited a small group of physicians to a meeting at Long Island College Hospital in Brooklyn, New York, to form the Long Island Society of Anesthetists — the first organized anesthesiology society in the United States, and only the second in the world after London's, founded in 1893. Eight physicians joined at a dollar a year, meeting monthly to discuss what was still, six decades after Ether Day, a largely improvised and under-studied branch of medicine, often assigned to whoever on the surgical team was most expendable. The society renamed itself the New York Society of Anesthetists in 1911, then the American Society of Anesthetists in 1936, and finally the American Society of Anesthesiologists in 1945 — the direct institutional ancestor of the group that will fill the San Diego Convention Center later this month for ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026. A hundred and twenty-one years on, the throughline from eight physicians in a Brooklyn hospital room to a 1,000-abstract annual meeting is worth a moment's notice. 🧠 Board Question of the Week Twelve minutes after an ultrasound-guided interscalene brachial plexus block with 30 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine, a patient becomes acutely confused, then develops perioral numbness followed by a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Oxygen saturation is 94% on room air and the patient is rapidly becoming bradycardic. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step? A Administer a benzodiazepine for seizure control and reassess in several minutes B Call for help, secure the airway with 100% oxygen, and administer 20% lipid emulsion while initiating ACLS modifications as needed C Administer naloxone and observe, since the presentation is most consistent with opioid-induced respiratory depression D Inject additional bupivacaine at the block site to "complete" the block and limit further systemic absorption Correct answer: B — this is local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), and lipid emulsion is first-line treatment The timing, CNS prodrome (confusion, perioral numbness), seizure, and cardiovascular instability following a large-volume bupivacaine block are classic for LAST — bupivacaine's high lipid solubility and potent sodium- and potassium-channel blockade make it especially prone to producing both seizures and malignant dysrhythmias when it reaches systemic circulation in sufficient concentration. Per ASRA's LAST checklist, management is airway management and oxygenation first (hypoxia and acidosis worsen local anesthetic cardiotoxicity), then prompt 20% lipid emulsion bolus (1.5 mL/kg lean body mass) followed by infusion, with ACLS modified to favor smaller epinephrine doses and to avoid vasopressin, calcium-channel blockers, and beta-blockers if cardiac arrest develops. A is incomplete: treating the seizure alone ignores the cardiovascular toxicity still building. C misreads the presentation — there's no indication of opioid exposure, and naloxone does nothing for LAST. D is actively harmful, since it only adds more local anesthetic to a patient already showing systemic toxicity. News-Medical.net · ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 to Highlight Latest Advances in Anesthesia Care · ASA · ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 Federal Workforce Analysts Put a Harder Number on the Anesthesia Shortage HRSA's Bureau of Health Workforce, via its National Center for Health Workforce Analysis, now projects a shortage of roughly 3,720 anesthesiologist full-time-equivalents nationally this year, widening to about 8,140 by 2031 as demand for surgical and procedural volume keeps outpacing new supply. A parallel industry workforce analysis puts the metro-area CRNA shortfall at around 3,140 FTEs for 2026, with the gap expected to persist through the decade. Roughly 30% of practicing anesthesiologists are projected to leave clinical practice by 2033, and more than 80% of rural U.S. counties already lack a practicing anesthesiologist at all, leaning even more heavily on CRNAs to cover the gap. The doctoral-degree requirement that took effect for new CRNAs in 2025 has also stretched training timelines, adding pressure on the supply side just as demand keeps climbing. AANA's letter argues nothing in CMS's proposed definition of "collaborator" should exclude nurse anesthesia practices. Time to intubation differed by only about 2.4 seconds — clinically negligible — and there were no meaningful differences in mortality or hospital length of stay. Notably, the authors' trial sequential analysis found the evidence base still falls short of the roughly 9,782 patients needed to call the first-attempt-success benefit conclusively proven, despite video laryngoscopy's now-widespread adoption. For SRNAs, it's a useful corrective: VL's advantage over DL in this population is real but smaller and less certain than routine practice might suggest, and where you intubate matters as much as what you intubate with. Semaglutide, tirzepatide, and liraglutide don't just lower glucose and suppress appetite — they slow gastric emptying, largely through vagally mediated effects on antral motility and pyloric tone, as part of the same mechanism that produces satiety. That delay is dose- and duration-dependent and doesn't reliably resolve with routine preoperative fasting: unlike a normal stomach, a GLP-1-slowed stomach may still hold solid contents after a standard 8-hour fast, even in an asymptomatic patient with no nausea, reflux, or early satiety to flag the risk. Case reports of aspiration during endoscopy and elective surgery in patients who followed standard NPO guidance are what pushed ASA and partner societies to abandon their original 2023 advice (hold the drug for a fixed number of days) in favor of a 2024 risk-stratified approach. Board-relevant pearl: the current multi-society guidance doesn't set a universal NPO extension — it asks the anesthesia team to screen for GI symptoms, consider point-of-care gastric ultrasound when available, and individualize the decision between proceeding, treating the patient as full-stomach (rapid-sequence induction or awake intubation), or delaying the case, rather than relying on days-since-last-dose alone. The underlying physiology — GLP-1 receptors slowing gastric motility through vagal and enteric pathways — is the testable concept; the clinical takeaway is that a reassuring fasting history doesn't rule out a full stomach in this population. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History September 30, 1811 On September 30, 1811, the English novelist Fanny Burney underwent a mastectomy in Paris for suspected breast cancer - fully conscious, with no anesthetic of any kind, thirty-five years before Morton's ether demonstration would make such an operation unthinkable to endure awake. Burney refused wine or opium beforehand, fearing they would dull her ability to cooperate with the surgeons. Seven men, including her husband, held her down as Baron Dominique-Jean Larrey, Napoleon's chief military surgeon, performed the excision with a team of assistants; Burney later described feeling the blade "cutting through veins - arteries - flesh - nerves" in a letter to her sister written nearly a year later, one of the most detailed first-person surgical accounts to survive from the pre-anesthetic era. She lived another 29 years. Her account is still cited in the history of medicine as a visceral reminder of exactly what ether, and everything that followed it, was invented to end. 🧠 Board Question of the Week During rapid-sequence induction for an emergent case, two attempts at direct laryngoscopy fail to visualize the glottis. Mask ventilation is difficult but still possible, and oxygen saturation has fallen to 89%. A video laryngoscope is immediately available at the bedside. What is the most appropriate next step? A Make a third attempt at direct laryngoscopy with a bougie, since additional attempts with the same technique improve the odds of success B Proceed immediately to surgical cricothyrotomy, since any oxygen desaturation during RSI mandates a surgical airway C Switch to video laryngoscopy as the next intubation attempt before escalating to a surgical airway D Hold all further airway attempts and wait for spontaneous ventilation to return Correct answer: C - escalate to a different, higher-yield technique before moving to a surgical airway This is a difficult airway with ongoing, if difficult, mask ventilation - not a "cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate" emergency. The ASA Difficult Airway Algorithm calls for limiting repeated attempts with a failing technique and escalating to a different device or approach while oxygenation can still be maintained. Video laryngoscopy improves glottic visualization by bypassing the need for a direct line of sight and, per recent meta-analysis data, modestly improves first-attempt success over direct laryngoscopy, particularly when a neuromuscular blocker is already on board - making it the logical next step here, before committing to an invasive surgical airway. A is wrong because repeating the same failed technique without changing anything meaningfully lowers, not raises, the odds of success and burns time and oxygen reserve. B is wrong because a surgical airway is reserved for a true "cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate" scenario — mask ventilation, though difficult, is still working here, so a less invasive rescue option should be tried first. D is wrong because this patient cannot be safely left unsecured with a desaturating, difficult airway; the algorithm calls for active escalation, not watchful waiting. Try again THE ETHER GAZETTE . A week later, the Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology, the Anesthesia Patient Safety Foundation, and ASA issued a joint statement reaffirming that properly administered spinal anesthesia remains safe and essential, while renewing calls for standardized, clearly labeled medications; physical separation of high-alert drugs from those intended for neuraxial use; and technology-assisted verification throughout pharmacy preparation, dispensing, and administration. The case has become a fast-moving case study in wrong-drug error prevention well beyond Nashville. A final rule is expected later this fall; for the second year running, hospital-based specialties including anesthesiology are bracing for real reimbursement pressure regardless of how CMS resolves the open comments. Sugammadex is a modified γ-cyclodextrin that reverses neuromuscular blockade by molecular encapsulation: its lipophilic core forms a tight 1:1 host–guest complex with the steroidal aminosteroid neuromuscular blockers rocuronium and, less efficiently, vecuronium, pulling free drug out of the neuromuscular junction and into plasma down a newly created concentration gradient. Cisatracurium and atracurium are benzylisoquinolinium blockers — a completely different molecular scaffold, lacking the steroid nucleus sugammadex's cavity is shaped to bind — so sugammadex has no meaningful reversal effect on them. With rocuronium supply under strain for years and Hospira's cisatracurium formulations now facing discontinuation, some centers are substituting between the two drug classes to preserve inventory; the substitution is not equivalent from a reversal standpoint. Board-relevant pearl: neostigmine (with glycopyrrolate) remains the only practical reversal option for benzylisoquinolinium blockers like cisatracurium, and it has a ceiling effect that sugammadex doesn't — as an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, neostigmine can only augment the acetylcholine already available at the junction, so reversing a deep block (TOF count 0–1) reliably requires some spontaneous recovery to already be underway. Sugammadex, by contrast, works independent of the patient's own recovery because it removes the blocking drug directly. This distinction — encapsulation versus enzyme inhibition — is one of the more commonly tested reversal-agent concepts on the boards, and it stops being academic the moment a formulary shortage forces a switch between drug classes mid-case. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History September 22, 1818 On September 22, 1818, an anonymous article appeared in the Quarterly Journal of Science and the Arts describing the curious, lethargic stupor that could be produced by inhaling ether vapor. Its author was a 26-year-old laboratory assistant named Michael Faraday, working under Humphry Davy at the Royal Institution — the same Davy who, two decades earlier, had first proposed nitrous oxide's potential to "annihilate physical pain" during surgery, only to see the idea shelved for a generation. Faraday's brief note observed that ether vapor, like nitrous oxide, could produce effects resembling intoxication, and that its inhalation deserved further study — but like Davy's nitrous oxide observation before it, the finding sat unused for nearly three decades. It would take until October 16, 1846, and William Morton's public demonstration at Massachusetts General Hospital, for ether's anesthetic potential to move from a laboratory curiosity to the operating room. Faraday went on to a career defined by electromagnetism, not medicine, but his 1818 footnote remains one of the earliest documented observations of the drug that gave this newsletter its name. 🧠 Board Question of the Week A 34-year-old patient with a T6 spinal cord injury sustained 10 weeks ago presents for urgent debridement of a sacral pressure ulcer. The surgical team requests a rapid-sequence induction. Which of the following is the most appropriate neuromuscular blocking agent choice, and why? A Succinylcholine, because its fast onset outweighs any hyperkalemia risk once an injury is subacute rather than acute B Rocuronium at a high intubating dose (1.2 mg/kg), because succinylcholine carries an unacceptable hyperkalemia risk well beyond the acute injury phase C Succinylcholine, because denervation-related hyperkalemia risk is confined to the first 24–48 hours after spinal cord injury D Vecuronium, because nondepolarizing agents are always preferred for rapid-sequence induction regardless of injury history Correct answer: B — a high-dose nondepolarizer is the standard alternative once succinylcholine is contraindicated Succinylcholine depolarizes the neuromuscular junction by binding acetylcholine receptors. After denervation injuries such as spinal cord injury, extrajunctional (immature-type) nicotinic receptors proliferate across the muscle membrane beginning roughly 3–5 days post-injury and persisting for many months, dramatically increasing the receptor pool succinylcholine can depolarize simultaneously. This produces an exaggerated, potentially life-threatening potassium efflux — hyperkalemic cardiac arrest has been reported with routine succinylcholine dosing in this population. At 10 weeks post-injury, this patient is squarely within the high-risk window, so succinylcholine should be avoided regardless of surgical urgency. A high-dose, rapid-onset nondepolarizing agent such as rocuronium (1.2 mg/kg) is the standard alternative for RSI when succinylcholine is contraindicated, accepting a longer duration of action that can, if needed, be shortened with sugammadex reversal. A is wrong because it inverts the actual risk pattern — succinylcholine's danger increases the further the injury is from truly hyperacute, not less. C is wrong because the vulnerable window begins days after injury, not within the first 24–48 hours, and can persist for many months; ten weeks is well within it. D is wrong because the answer's reasoning is an overly broad, untrue categorical claim — the relevant point isn't that nondepolarizers are "always" preferred for RSI, it's why succinylcholine specifically is dangerous in this patient. Local anesthetics are weak bases that exist in solution as an equilibrium between a charged (protonated, ionized) form and an uncharged (nonionized) form. Only the uncharged form is lipid-soluble enough to cross the nerve's lipid membrane in meaningful quantity — so the closer a drug's pKa sits to physiologic pH (7.4), the larger its nonionized fraction at injection, and the faster its clinical onset. Lidocaine (pKa ≈7.9) and mepivacaine (pKa ≈7.6) act quickly for exactly this reason, while bupivacaine (pKa ≈8.1) is comparatively slower. Once inside the axoplasm, the drug re-ionizes and it's the charged form that actually plugs the intracellular gate of the voltage-gated sodium channel, blocking Na⁺ influx and preventing action-potential propagation — so onset speed and the actual blocking mechanism depend on two different forms of the same molecule. Board-relevant pearl: potency and lipid solubility travel together (more lipid-soluble agents partition more readily into the nerve membrane and into cardiac tissue), and it's exactly this property that makes bupivacaine more cardiotoxic than lidocaine at equipotent doses. Bupivacaine binds cardiac sodium channels with markedly slower dissociation kinetics — the classic "fast-in, slow-out" description — so it accumulates in the channel between heartbeats at clinically relevant heart rates, producing refractory ventricular arrhythmias that are disproportionately hard to resuscitate compared with lidocaine toxicity. That pharmacologic detail is the entire reason ASRA's local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) checklist treats bupivacaine-associated cardiac arrest differently from a routine ACLS code. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History September 15, 1884 On September 15, 1884, the world learned that cocaine could numb a nerve. Carl Koller, a young Viennese ophthalmology resident, had spent weeks searching for a way to anesthetize the eye for surgery, after a colleague — Sigmund Freud, then pursuing cocaine's psychiatric potential — mentioned the drug's numbing effect on the tongue. Koller dissolved cocaine in water, dripped it into a frog's eye, then a rabbit's, then his own, and confirmed he could touch the cornea with a pin and feel nothing. Too poor to afford travel to the Heidelberg Ophthalmological Society's congress, Koller had a colleague, Josef Brettauer, read his findings to the assembled ophthalmologists on his behalf. The report ignited immediate excitement across surgical specialties — within months, surgeons worldwide were experimenting with cocaine for nerve blocks, and within a decade the search for a less toxic, non-addictive alternative had begun, eventually yielding procaine and the modern amide and ester local anesthetics SRNAs use today. Koller's own reward was more complicated: he emigrated to New York in 1888 after a duel over the priority dispute, and cocaine's addictive and cardiotoxic properties — including Freud's own struggles with it — became one of the field's earliest lessons in taking a "safe" new drug's dangers seriously. 🧠 Board Question of the Week Fifteen minutes into an ultrasound-guided interscalene block using 30 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine, a patient reports circumoral numbness and tinnitus, then becomes acutely agitated and has a witnessed generalized seizure. Shortly after, the patient becomes bradycardic and hypotensive. In addition to airway management and seizure control, which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment? A A full resuscitative dose of intravenous epinephrine (1 mg), per standard ACLS cardiac arrest dosing B 20% intravenous lipid emulsion, given as a bolus followed by a continuous infusion per the ASRA LAST checklist C Intravenous verapamil to control the emerging bradyarrhythmia D A second, smaller dose of bupivacaine to "reset" the local nerve block before further workup Correct answer: B — 20% lipid emulsion is first-line therapy for local anesthetic systemic toxicity This presentation — perioral numbness and tinnitus progressing to seizure, followed by cardiovascular collapse — is the classic evolution of local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) from intravascular or excessive systemic absorption of a large-volume block, and bupivacaine's slow dissociation from cardiac sodium channels makes it especially dangerous once cardiotoxicity begins. ASRA's LAST checklist calls for immediate 20% lipid emulsion — an initial bolus followed by an infusion — on top of airway management and seizure control, based on the "lipid sink" mechanism in which the emulsion sequesters the lipophilic local anesthetic away from cardiac tissue and may also improve myocardial energy substrate delivery. A is wrong because ASRA specifically recommends reducing individual epinephrine doses (to ≤1 mcg/kg) during LAST resuscitation rather than giving standard ACLS boluses, since large doses of epinephrine have been associated with worse outcomes and impaired lipid resuscitation in animal models of bupivacaine toxicity. C is wrong because calcium channel blockers and beta blockers are specifically avoided in LAST — they compound the myocardial depression already caused by the local anesthetic. D is wrong and dangerous: giving additional local anesthetic during an evolving toxic reaction adds more drug to an already toxic systemic load. Unlike GABAergic agents, which produce global cortical depression, ketamine is a noncompetitive antagonist at the NMDA glutamate receptor. Blocking NMDA receptors functionally disconnects the thalamocortical pathways from the limbic system, producing what's classically termed "dissociative anesthesia": a trance-like, cataleptic state in which the patient appears disconnected from their surroundings rather than unconscious in the propofol sense. Because ketamine doesn't suppress the brainstem respiratory centers or the airway-protective reflexes the way GABAergic agents do, spontaneous ventilation and airway tone are typically preserved even at induction doses — part of why it remains a go-to agent for austere or prehospital settings, pediatric procedural sedation, and patients you don't want to fully paralyze and intubate. Board-relevant pearl: know why ketamine's hemodynamic profile isn't as reliable as its reputation suggests. Ketamine indirectly raises heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac output by inhibiting neuronal reuptake of norepinephrine — an indirect sympathomimetic effect, not direct receptor agonism. That effect depends on the patient having intact catecholamine stores to release. In a patient who has been in prolonged shock, sepsis, or another catecholamine-depleted state, those stores can be exhausted, unmasking ketamine's own intrinsic direct myocardial depressant effect — meaning the same drug that reliably raises blood pressure in a healthy trauma patient can drop it in a chronically critically ill one. This is exactly the kind of exception that shows up on exams precisely because it contradicts the "ketamine is always hemodynamically stable" teaching point. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History September 10, 1862 On September 10, 1862, James Tayloe Gwathmey was born in Roanoke, Virginia — an unlikely start for a man later called the "Father of Modern Anesthesia." Before medicine, Gwathmey was expelled from the Virginia Military Institute, joined an acrobatic troupe, and taught gymnastics at YMCAs in Iowa and Nebraska. He didn't earn his M.D. from Vanderbilt until 1899, at nearly 37. Moving to New York City in 1902, he made a deliberate and at-the-time unusual choice: he built one of the first full-time private anesthesia practices in the country, establishing clinical independence from the surgeons he worked alongside — a professional stance that still echoes in how anesthesia providers, physician and CRNA alike, think about their relationship to surgical teams today. That mechanism requires the patient to have endogenous catecholamine stores available to release. In a patient who has been in shock for an extended period, those stores can already be significantly depleted, unmasking ketamine's own intrinsic direct negative inotropic effect on the myocardium — producing hypotension instead of the expected pressor response. This is a well-recognized exception to the "ketamine is hemodynamically stable" teaching point and a common way exam writers test whether a candidate understands the mechanism rather than just the reputation. A is wrong because ketamine's cardiovascular stimulation is indirect (via catecholamine reuptake inhibition), not direct receptor agonism. B is wrong because ketamine does have a direct myocardial depressant effect — it's simply overshadowed by the indirect sympathomimetic effect in patients with normal catecholamine reserves. Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective α2-adrenergic agonist — roughly eight times more α2-selective than clonidine — that acts primarily at the locus coeruleus in the brainstem. Stimulating α2 receptors there hyperpolarizes noradrenergic neurons, shutting down the tonic norepinephrine output that normally keeps the cortex aroused, which disinhibits the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus and produces a sedative state that resembles natural non-REM sleep far more closely than a GABAergic drug like propofol does. Because the sedation isn't routed through GABA-A receptors, ventilatory drive is largely preserved even at clinically effective doses — the main reason dexmedetomidine has become a favored adjunct for awake fiberoptic intubation and sedation cases where spontaneous ventilation and airway reflexes need to stay intact. Board-relevant pearl: know dexmedetomidine's biphasic hemodynamic signature. A loading dose can transiently activate peripheral postsynaptic α2B receptors on vascular smooth muscle, producing brief hypertension with reflex bradycardia, before the drug's dominant central α2A-mediated sympatholysis takes over and produces the more familiar steady-state hypotension and bradycardia. On an exam — or at the bedside — a patient who gets hypertensive right after a dexmedetomidine bolus isn't having a paradoxical reaction; that's the expected peripheral phase, and it's a reason to load slowly (or skip the bolus) in patients who can't tolerate the swing. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History September 7, 1922 On September 7, 1922, William Stewart Halsted died in Baltimore — remembered today as the father of the American surgical residency system, but also, less famously, one of the founders of regional anesthesia. In 1884, after reading Carl Koller's report that cocaine could numb the eye for ophthalmic surgery, Halsted and several colleagues began injecting cocaine directly into peripheral nerves on themselves and each other, systematically mapping out what became the first true nerve-block techniques — direct ancestors of the brachial plexus and intercostal blocks taught in every regional-anesthesia rotation today. The self-experimentation exacted a brutal personal toll: Halsted developed a lifelong cocaine addiction that nearly derailed his career, and his attempt to treat it left him dependent on morphine for the rest of his life, a struggle he largely concealed while building Johns Hopkins's surgical program into a national model. It's a legacy worth sitting with alongside the technique itself — regional anesthesia's earliest history is inseparable from the people who tested it on their own bodies first, often at real personal cost. 🧠 Board Question of the Week A 19-year-old man develops masseter muscle rigidity, tachycardia to the 140s, and rapidly rising end-tidal CO 2 shortly after induction with succinylcholine and sevoflurane for an emergency appendectomy. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacologic intervention? A Intravenous dantrolene, 2.5 mg/kg, repeated as needed B Intravenous calcium chloride, 10 mg/kg C Switch to a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker and continue the case D Intravenous physostigmine, 1–2 mg Correct answer: A — dantrolene is the only agent that reverses the underlying process in malignant hyperthermia This presentation — masseter rigidity, tachycardia, and a rapidly rising end-tidal CO 2 shortly after exposure to succinylcholine and a volatile agent — is classic for malignant hyperthermia (MH). Dantrolene works by binding the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle, blocking the pathological calcium release that drives the hypermetabolic crisis, and restoring normal excitation-contraction coupling. It's the only pharmacologic agent proven to reverse MH and should be dosed at 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated as needed up to a cumulative 10 mg/kg, alongside stopping all triggering agents and initiating standard MH-crisis supportive care. B is wrong because calcium chloride treats the cardiotoxicity of hyperkalemia — a downstream complication of MH, not the underlying mechanism — and giving calcium can actually worsen the intracellular calcium overload that's driving the crisis. C is wrong because continuing the case ignores the emergency: triggering agents must be stopped immediately and the case aborted, or converted to a non-triggering technique, once the patient is stabilized. D is wrong because physostigmine reverses anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) delirium, a different clinical picture entirely, and has no role in treating MH. Clear, non-particulate liquids (water, pulp-free juice, black coffee, sports drinks) empty from the stomach largely by first-order kinetics driven by volume and hydrostatic pressure, with a half-emptying time typically under 15 minutes regardless of whether the starting volume was 150 mL or 450 mL — residual volume converges back toward a low fasting baseline well within an hour for most patients. That's mechanistically different from solids, fats, and protein-containing liquids like milk, which trigger antral grinding, pyloric sieving, and duodenal feedback inhibition that can stretch gastric emptying out past four to six hours. ASA and European (ESAIC) guidance has permitted clear liquids up to two hours before elective anesthesia for years; the data in this issue's Literature pick is pushing programs to ask whether even that two-hour buffer is doing much beyond making patients thirstier — particularly in pediatrics, where dehydration and hypoglycemia from prolonged fasting are a bigger day-to-day problem than a hypothetical aspiration the volume-and-timing data doesn't support. Board-relevant distinction: know the classic 2-4-6-8 fasting rule (clears–breast milk–infant formula/light meal–solids/full meal), but also know why clear liquids get the shortest window — NPO status is fundamentally a volume-and-acidity risk model, and clear liquids fail to accumulate stomach volume the way solids do. On an exam, don't conflate "recent PO intake" (a genuine aspiration risk factor regardless of what any guideline says) with "guideline non-compliance" (missed the stated fasting window) — the former calls for a full-stomach precaution; the latter, in an otherwise low-risk elective case, often doesn't. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History August 29, 1809 On August 29, 1809, Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. was born in Cambridge, Massachusetts — the physician, essayist, and Harvard anatomy professor who, in a November 21, 1846 letter to William T. SGLT2 inhibitors — empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, and others — block glucose reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule, producing glycosuria, mild volume contraction, and a metabolic shift toward fat oxidation and ketogenesis, the same mechanism behind their renal- and cardio-protective effects (see this week's Literature pick). Under the physiologic stress of surgery — fasting, insulin withdrawal, catecholamine surge — that shift can tip into ketoacidosis, but because the drug's glycosuric effect keeps blood glucose from climbing, patients can present with a significant anion-gap ketoacidosis while their glucose reads a deceptively normal 130–180 mg/dL. Providers trained to equate DKA with a glucose in the 400s can miss it entirely. The practical takeaways: hold SGLT2 inhibitors before elective surgery per current guidance (traditionally 3–4 days, though emerging evidence questions whether shorter holds suffice), ask specifically about SGLT2-inhibitor use during the preoperative workup since patients don't always volunteer it, and if a postoperative patient develops unexplained nausea, tachypnea, or malaise, check a basic metabolic panel and ketones or pH even when the fingerstick glucose looks reassuring. A Obtain an MRI of the brain to rule out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis before proceeding further B Perform an epidural blood patch — the definitive treatment for a postural headache consistent with postdural puncture headache that has failed conservative management C Start empiric IV antibiotics for presumed bacterial meningitis D Reassure the patient that the headache will resolve on its own within 24–48 hours and discharge her home Correct answer: B — Epidural blood patch is the definitive treatment once conservative therapy fails The clinical picture — a positional headache dramatically worse upright and improved supine, developing within days of dural puncture, without fever — is classic for postdural puncture headache (PDPH). Ongoing CSF leak through the dural defect lowers intracranial pressure and causes traction on pain-sensitive meninges when upright. Conservative measures are reasonable first-line steps, but once they fail after 24–48 hours, an epidural blood patch — injecting 15–20 mL of the patient's own blood into the epidural space near the puncture site to form a clot that seals the leak — is the definitive treatment, effective in roughly 70–90% of cases after a single patch. A is a reasonable consideration if the headache doesn't fit the classic positional pattern or red flags emerge, but it isn't the next step for a textbook-positional PDPH that has already failed conservative therapy. C jumps to treating meningitis without supporting signs — no fever, and the positional quality argues strongly against it — though this week's headlines are a reminder that contaminated neuraxial injectate can cause genuine meningitis, that presentation doesn't fit a purely positional, afebrile headache. D under-treats a patient who has already failed conservative management and is suffering a debilitating, functionally disabling headache. Etomidate potentiates GABA-A receptor chloride currents like other induction agents, producing rapid hypnosis with minimal effect on myocardial contractility, systemic vascular resistance, or heart rate - the reason it remains a go-to induction agent for hemodynamically unstable, cardiac, and trauma patients even as broader anesthetic choices narrow this year (see this week's Drug Shortage Watch). That same stability comes with a well-known cost: etomidate reversibly inhibits 11β-hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol in the adrenal cortex, suppressing endogenous cortisol synthesis for roughly 6–8 hours after even a single induction dose. The suppression is usually clinically silent after a single bolus in an otherwise healthy patient, but it's why etomidate infusions fell out of favor for ICU sedation and why critically ill or septic patients who receive even one induction dose are sometimes considered for stress-dose steroid coverage. Etomidate's other signature quirks - myoclonus on induction (not seizure activity, though it can look like one), a comparatively high incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting, and pain on injection - are all worth anticipating regardless of the adrenal question. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History August 10, 1898 In Greifswald, Germany, surgeon August Bier administered what is generally credited as the first spinal anesthetic given specifically to enable surgery: a solution of cocaine injected into the subarachnoid space of his assistant, August Hildebrandt, after an earlier attempt on a patient had failed when too much of the drug leaked from a loose-fitting syringe. Bier and Hildebrandt then tested the block on each other - reportedly checking pain tolerance with pinpricks, cigar burns, and blows to the shin - in a demonstration that reads more like a dare than a clinical trial by modern standards. Both men suffered severe post-dural-puncture headaches for days afterward, an early and unintentional demonstration of the complication that would occupy anesthesia researchers for the next century. MH is caused by a defect, most commonly in the RYR1 gene, that leaves the ryanodine receptor abnormally sensitive to triggering agents (all volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine), producing uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and a hypermetabolic cascade. C treats a downstream consequence - hyperkalemia - rather than the underlying calcium dysregulation, and isn't first-line; standard hyperkalemia measures are adjuncts once dantrolene is underway, not substitutes for it. D does nothing to interrupt the hypermetabolic process driving the tachycardia and would delay definitive treatment. LAST results from unintentional intravascular injection or excessive systemic absorption of local anesthetic, producing a spectrum from perioral numbness and tinnitus to seizures and, in the most severe cases, cardiovascular collapse. Cardiac arrest can be the presenting sign with bupivacaine specifically, because its high protein binding and lipophilicity let it linger in cardiac tissue and block sodium channels longer than lidocaine does. CNS warning signs may be masked entirely under general anesthesia or heavy sedation, so cardiovascular instability out of proportion to the clinical picture should raise suspicion for LAST on its own. Treatment starts with stopping the injection, calling for help, and securing the airway with 100% oxygen — preventing the acidosis and hypoxia that worsen toxicity — followed immediately by 20% lipid emulsion: a 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then a continuous infusion, per the current ASRA checklist. Avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, and beta blockers, which ASRA's guideline flags as harmful in this setting, and be prepared for a prolonged resuscitation — LAST-related cardiac arrest can require chest compressions well past the usual ACLS endpoints while the lipid emulsion takes effect. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History August 9, 1819 William Thomas Green Morton, the Boston dentist who gave the world its first successful public demonstration of surgical anesthesia, was born in Charlton, Massachusetts. Twenty-seven years later, on October 16, 1846, Morton administered ether to patient Edward Gilbert Abbott in the Bulfinch Building amphitheater at Massachusetts General Hospital — now nicknamed the "Ether Dome" — while surgeon John Collins Warren removed a vascular tumor from Abbott's neck. Warren's reported remark to the assembled crowd, "Gentlemen, this is no humbug," marked the moment surgical pain stopped being an unavoidable cost of survival. Morton spent much of his later life in patent disputes over the discovery — he'd tried to market ether anesthesia commercially under the name "Letheon" — and died largely impoverished in 1868, but the October demonstration remains the date the profession marks as anesthesia's public birth, with Morton's August birthday a quieter footnote in the same story. 🧠 Board Question of the Week A 34-year-old man with a T6 spinal cord injury sustained three weeks ago presents for incision and drainage of a sacral abscess. The surgeon requests rapid-sequence induction. Which of the following neuromuscular blocking agent choices is most appropriate, and why? A Succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg — its rapid onset and short duration make it ideal for RSI regardless of injury timeline B Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg — succinylcholine can produce life-threatening hyperkalemia beginning roughly 24–72 hours after a denervation injury and persisting for 6–9 months or longer C Succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg — it's safe here because the injury is spinal cord, not peripheral nerve D Cisatracurium 0.15 mg/kg — it has the fastest onset of any non-depolarizing agent, matching succinylcholine's speed without the risk Correct answer: B — High-dose rocuronium matches succinylcholine's speed without the hyperkalemia risk Denervation injuries — spinal cord injury, burns, prolonged immobility, stroke, Guillain-Barré syndrome — trigger proliferation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors across the affected muscle membrane. Succinylcholine's depolarization of that expanded receptor field can release enough potassium to cause cardiac arrest, with risk beginning around 24–72 hours post-injury and persisting for many months until the receptor upregulation resolves. Rocuronium at 1.2 mg/kg achieves an onset (roughly 60 seconds) comparable to succinylcholine, making it the standard substitute for RSI in this population. C is wrong because spinal cord injury produces the same extrajunctional receptor proliferation below the level of injury as peripheral denervation does — the risk isn't limited to peripheral nerve damage. D's premise is simply false: rocuronium, not cisatracurium, is the fastest-onset non-depolarizing agent, which is exactly why rocuronium — not cisatracurium — is the go-to RSI substitute when succinylcholine is contraindicated. This week's FDA alert on sevoflurane is a sharp reminder that volatile anesthetics aren't metabolically inert. Mitochondria generate the ATP that excitable, oxygen-hungry tissue — brain and heart chief among it — depends on minute to minute, and volatile agents are known to mildly suppress mitochondrial electron transport chain activity as part of how they produce anesthesia. In a patient with a normal mitochondrial reserve, that suppression is trivial and fully reversible. In a patient carrying a pathogenic mitochondrial variant — like the MT-ND4 m.11232T>C mutation implicated in the current cases — baseline oxidative capacity is already reduced, and volatile-agent suppression on top of that can tip vulnerable tissue into energy failure, producing exactly the picture being reported: unexplained neurologic devastation or cardiac collapse in patients with no other risk factors. The practical takeaway for boards and bedside alike isn't "avoid volatiles in everyone" — it's recognizing when mitochondrial disease is on the differential (unexplained lactic acidosis, myopathy, prior anesthetic complications, suggestive family or ancestry history) and defaulting toward total intravenous or regional techniques in those patients, since propofol and regional anesthesia don't carry the same electron-transport-chain liability at clinical doses. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History July 25, 1894 Harold Griffith was born in Montreal on this date — the anesthetist who, on January 23, 1942, gave the world its first practical neuromuscular blocking agent. Working with resident Enid Johnson at the Homeopathic Hospital of Montreal, Griffith injected an extract of curare, Intocostrin , into a 20-year-old undergoing an appendectomy, producing profound muscle relaxation without deepening the ether anesthesia already in progress. Before that afternoon, adequate relaxation for abdominal surgery meant anesthetizing patients dangerously deep; Griffith's report, published later that year, opened the door to lighter, safer anesthesia paired with deliberate paralysis — the conceptual split between hypnosis, analgesia, and relaxation that still organizes how anesthesia is taught today. Griffith went on to introduce cyclopropane to Canadian practice, establish the country's first postoperative recovery room, and serve as founding president of the World Federation of Societies of Anaesthesiologists. 🧠 Board Question of the Week In the PACU, a patient extubated 20 minutes ago after a laparoscopic case involving rocuronium develops intermittent upper-airway obstruction, uncoordinated jerky limb movements, and difficulty maintaining a sustained head lift. A qualitative peripheral nerve stimulator shows a train-of-four with no fade appreciable to the observer. Which statement best describes this scenario? A Residual neuromuscular blockade has been definitively ruled out because the train-of-four shows no fade B Clinically significant residual blockade can still be present; qualitative train-of-four monitoring reliably detects fade only once the train-of-four ratio has fallen below about 0.4, well short of the 0.9 threshold associated with these symptoms C These findings are more consistent with emergence delirium than with neuromuscular blockade D A normal train-of-four by any method excludes residual paralysis as a cause of postoperative airway obstruction Correct answer: B — Qualitative TOF can look reassuring while real residual blockade persists The vignette describes classic signs of residual neuromuscular blockade: upper-airway obstruction, uncoordinated movement, and inability to sustain a head lift — a bedside surrogate for a train-of-four ratio below roughly 0.9, the threshold below which pharyngeal function and airway protection are impaired. The trap in this question is the "normal" qualitative TOF: the human eye reliably detects fade only when the train-of-four ratio has already dropped well below 0.4, so a qualitative twitch monitor can look unremarkable at ratios between roughly 0.4 and 0.9 — precisely the range where clinically meaningful residual paralysis lives. This gap is the rationale behind APSF's ongoing push for quantitative neuromuscular monitoring (which reports an actual numeric TOF ratio) as the more reliable standard before extubation. Emergence delirium doesn't produce upper-airway obstruction or an inability to sustain a head lift as its primary features, so C is a weaker fit for this clinical picture. D repeats the same qualitative-versus-quantitative trap as A — a "normal" TOF by qualitative assessment never fully excludes clinically important residual blockade, whereas a quantitative TOF ratio at or above 0.9 does. Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) starts with CNS signs — perioral numbness, tinnitus, a metallic taste, agitation — and can progress within minutes to seizures and, in the worst cases, cardiovascular collapse that's notoriously resistant to standard ACLS. Bupivacaine is the classic villain: highly lipophilic and tightly protein-bound, it partitions into cardiac tissue and blocks myocardial sodium channels longer and more potently than less lipophilic agents like lidocaine or ropivacaine. The fix is almost as counterintuitive as the injury: 20% IV lipid emulsion, given as a 1.5 mL/kg bolus followed by a 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion. The leading explanation is the "lipid sink" — an expanded intravascular lipid phase that pulls lipophilic local anesthetic molecules out of cardiac tissue and plasma faster than they can act — alongside a proposed direct metabolic and inotropic effect on stressed myocardium. Per ASRA's LAST checklist, propofol is not an acceptable substitute for lipid emulsion (its lipid content is too low and its cardiodepressant effects work against you), and standard resuscitation doses of epinephrine should be reduced, since large boluses appear to worsen outcomes in LAST-associated arrest. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History July 25, 1834 On this date, the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge died in London at 61 — best remembered for "Kubla Khan" and "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner," but also, decades earlier, an eager volunteer in one of anesthesia's true prehistory experiments. Coleridge described a sensation of "highly pleasurable thrilling" throughout his limbs, and Davy — who nearly injured himself testing gases on his own body throughout the project — went on to note, almost as an aside in his 1800 research volume, that nitrous oxide "appears capable of destroying physical pain" and might be used "with advantage during surgical operations." ASRA's LAST checklist calls for airway management, seizure suppression with a benzodiazepine, and 20% lipid emulsion as first-line treatment: a 1.5 mL/kg bolus (roughly 100 mL in an average adult), repeatable up to twice for persistent cardiovascular collapse, followed by an infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min until hemodynamic stability is restored. Standard ACLS epinephrine doses should be reduced (to boluses of ≤1 mcg/kg) rather than given at full resuscitation doses, since case and animal data suggest large doses impair resuscitation from LAST-associated arrest. MH is triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine in genetically susceptible patients (most often via RYR1 mutations), causing the ryanodine receptor on the sarcoplasmic reticulum to dump calcium into the muscle cytoplasm uncontrollably. That flood of calcium drives sustained contraction, runaway heat production, and skyrocketing oxygen consumption — the hypermetabolic state that produces the classic triad of rising end-tidal CO2, muscle rigidity, and fever. Dantrolene binds the RYR1 receptor directly and blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, cutting off the process at its source rather than just treating the downstream fever or acidosis. Initial dosing is 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated every 5–10 minutes until symptoms resolve — there is no fixed maximum in an ongoing crisis. Because a single reaction doesn't fully rule a patient out or in, current guidance leans on a short screening history (personal or family MH reaction, and any prior genetic testing) to decide who actually needs formal RYR1 / CACNA1S / STAC3 sequencing, rather than testing everyone with a vague family rumor of "anesthesia problems." 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History June 17, 1931 On June 17, 1931, Agatha Hodgins founded the National Association of Nurse Anesthetists — the organization that would become today's AANA — in Cleveland, Ohio. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management, assuming the airway is secured and seizure activity is controlled? A Administer high-dose epinephrine (1 mg IV) per standard ACLS arrest dosing B Give a second local anesthetic bolus through the catheter to "burn off" the receptor C Begin 20% lipid emulsion therapy (bolus followed by continuous infusion) D Administer flumazenil to reverse the neurologic toxicity Correct answer: C — Begin 20% lipid emulsion therapy This presentation is classic local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST): early CNS signs (perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste) progressing to seizure, which can precede cardiovascular collapse. Per ASRA's LAST checklist, once the airway/seizure is managed, first-line treatment is 20% lipid emulsion — typically a 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 2–3 minutes followed by a 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion — which acts as a "lipid sink," partitioning lipophilic local anesthetic away from cardiac and neural tissue. A is wrong because ACLS-dose epinephrine (versus the reduced <1 mcg/kg boluses ASRA recommends in LAST) can worsen arrhythmias and impair lipid resuscitation. B is wrong and dangerous — more local anesthetic deepens toxicity. D treats benzodiazepine toxicity, not LAST, and doesn't address the underlying problem.
